title: Deep Learning Fundamentals
blurb: The mechanics of neural networks before transformers entered the building. Backprop, optimization, the architectures that came before — and the early generative ideas that still echo in 2026.

nodes.label: Neural nets as computational graphs
nodes.description: A neural network is a graph of differentiable operations. This mental model — not 'neurons' — is what carries you all the way to transformers.
nodes.doneWhen: You can draw the forward and backward computational graph of a 2-layer MLP and a 1-D conv.

resources.title: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero — micrograd
resources.author: Andrej Karpathy
resources.annotation: Builds a working autograd in 100 lines on video. The clearest 'computational graph' tutorial that exists.

resources.title: Deep Learning
resources.author: Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville
resources.annotation: The MIT Press canonical reference, free online. Chapter 6 is the formal treatment of feedforward nets and computational graphs.

resources.title: Dive into Deep Learning (D2L)
resources.author: Zhang, Lipton, Li, Smola
resources.annotation: Free interactive textbook. Code-first; every concept comes with a notebook you can run.

nodes.label: Backpropagation
nodes.description: The chain rule applied at scale. Implement it once by hand on a tiny example so it stops feeling like magic.
nodes.doneWhen: You can implement a 2-layer net's forward and backward pass from scratch in NumPy.

resources.title: Yes you should understand backprop
resources.author: Andrej Karpathy
resources.annotation: Why backprop's leaky abstraction matters in practice. Read after you've coded a backward pass yourself.

resources.title: CS231n notes — Backpropagation
resources.author: Andrej Karpathy
resources.annotation: The classic Stanford notes. Walks the computation graph for a real example with index gymnastics.

nodes.label: Optimizers (SGD, momentum, Adam) & lr schedules
nodes.description: Plain SGD, momentum, Nesterov, Adam, AdamW, learning-rate schedules (cosine, warmup, linear decay). The choices that decide whether a model trains at all.
nodes.doneWhen: You can pick an optimizer and lr schedule for a new model and defend the choice.

resources.title: An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms
resources.author: Sebastian Ruder
resources.annotation: Side-by-side comparison of every optimizer with intuition. Dated on the frontier but still the canonical map.

resources.title: Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization
resources.author: Loshchilov & Hutter
resources.annotation: The AdamW paper. Required reading because AdamW is the default for every transformer in 2026.

resources.title: PyTorch — torch.optim
resources.annotation: The reference for every optimizer and lr scheduler you'll touch. Read the lr-scheduler section once.

nodes.label: Initialization & normalization
nodes.description: Xavier / He initialization, batch norm, layer norm, RMS norm. Why a model that won't train is usually a normalization-or-init problem.
nodes.doneWhen: You can explain why layer norm replaced batch norm in transformers.

resources.title: Delving Deep into Rectifiers
resources.author: He et al.
resources.annotation: The He-initialization paper. Short and worth the read; the math motivates why init matters more than people expect.

resources.title: Layer Normalization
resources.author: Ba, Kiros, Hinton
resources.annotation: The paper. Pair with the BatchNorm and RMSNorm papers — the contrast is what makes it click.

resources.title: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization
resources.author: Zhang & Sennrich
resources.annotation: RMSNorm — the norm of choice in most 2026 LLMs. The paper explains why dropping the mean is fine.

nodes.label: Activations & loss functions
nodes.description: ReLU, GELU, SwiGLU, sigmoid, softmax; MSE, cross-entropy, contrastive losses. Which one to use and when.
nodes.doneWhen: You can match an activation and loss to a task type without thinking.

resources.title: GLU Variants Improve Transformer
resources.author: Noam Shazeer
resources.annotation: Why SwiGLU is the activation of choice in modern transformers. A two-page paper; read it.

resources.title: PyTorch — Loss Functions
resources.annotation: The reference catalog. Use it to discover the losses you didn't know you needed (e.g., NLLLoss vs CrossEntropyLoss).

nodes.label: Convolutional neural networks
nodes.description: Conv, pooling, the standard CNN architectures (ResNet, EfficientNet). Even in 2026, CNNs win on edge vision and inside multi-modal stacks.
nodes.doneWhen: You can train a small CNN on CIFAR-10 and explain its receptive field.

resources.title: Stanford CS231n — Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition
resources.annotation: The course that taught a generation of researchers CNNs. The notes alone are worth a full pass.

resources.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (ResNet)
resources.author: He et al.
resources.annotation: ResNet. The residual-connection idea outlasted CNN dominance and now lives inside every transformer block.

nodes.label: RNNs & LSTMs (historical)
nodes.description: How sequences were modeled before attention. Mostly historical now, but the vocabulary still shows up. Skim, don't dwell.
nodes.doneWhen: You can explain in one sentence why transformers replaced RNNs for long sequences.

resources.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks
resources.author: Andrej Karpathy
resources.annotation: The classic post. Historical context, but useful intuition for why sequence modeling was hard before transformers.

resources.title: Understanding LSTM Networks
resources.author: Christopher Olah
resources.annotation: The canonical visual explainer. Skim once and move on; mostly history in 2026.

nodes.label: Embeddings & representation learning
nodes.description: Words, tokens, items, users — all as vectors in a learned space. word2vec, fastText, sentence embeddings. The bridge to retrieval and RAG.
nodes.doneWhen: You can compute cosine similarity between sentence embeddings and reason about the geometry.

resources.title: The Illustrated Word2vec
resources.author: Jay Alammar
resources.annotation: The visual intro to word embeddings — and by extension to every dense embedding you'll use later.

resources.title: Sentence-Transformers — official site
resources.annotation: The practical entry point. Pretrained sentence embedding models with one-line APIs; the basis of most RAG stacks.

resources.title: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) Leaderboard
resources.annotation: The current state of the embedding-model field. Pick by task; the top models change every few months.

nodes.label: Attention (the pre-transformer history)
nodes.description: Bahdanau attention, Luong attention, the seq2seq with attention era. Useful context for understanding why the transformer was a leap.
nodes.doneWhen: You can describe what 'attention' added to seq2seq before the transformer paper.

resources.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
resources.author: Bahdanau, Cho, Bengio
resources.annotation: The Bahdanau paper — the introduction of attention to neural sequence models. Read for historical context.

resources.title: Attention? Attention!
resources.author: Lilian Weng
resources.annotation: The pre-transformer attention zoo, summarized with care. Pair with the Bahdanau paper.

nodes.label: Generative models (overview)
nodes.description: Autoencoders, VAEs, GANs, diffusion. An overview, not a deep dive — enough to recognize them and connect them to the LLM-and-multimodal world that follows.
nodes.doneWhen: You can sketch the training objective of each family in one sentence.

resources.title: Lilian Weng's blog — From Autoencoder to Beta-VAE
resources.author: Lilian Weng
resources.annotation: The clearest VAE primer on the open web. Skim her blog for the GAN and diffusion posts too.

resources.title: What are Diffusion Models?
resources.author: Lilian Weng
resources.annotation: The reference intro. Survives every diffusion revision because the foundations are unchanged.

resources.title: Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.author: Goodfellow et al.
resources.annotation: The original GAN paper. Mostly historical now but the adversarial framing keeps showing up.
